category: war, capitulation, and end of a Muslim polity
location: Emirate of Granada (Nasrid kingdom), southern Iberia; the surrender at the city of Granada

date.note: The year given is that of the surrender of the city (2 January 1492); the preceding Granada War, from the Castilian seizure of Alhama in 1482 to the siege of the capital in 1491, is treated as background. The Capitulations were agreed in late 1491 (the earlier Castilian text is dated 25 November 1491). The Castilian court chronicle is loose on the sequence: it says the fortresses were handed over 'en los treinta de Deciembre', that their handover had been agreed for 'el dia de los Reyes', and then narrates the king's coming to the city on 2 January 1492, the date given here; the narrative in al-Maqqari dates Muhammad XII's departure from the Alhambra to 2 Rabi' I 897 AH, which Gayangos converts as 3 January. The same narrative dates Muhammad XII's death in Fez to 940 AH, which corresponds to 1533-34 CE; Gayangos converts it as A.D. 1538 (vol. 2, p. 390). The range is extended to 1502 to cover the breach of the terms: the forced baptisms in Granada from 1499, the risings of 1499-1501, and the Castilian order of February 1502 requiring the Muslims of Castile to accept baptism or leave.

summary: The Fall of Granada was the conquest of the Nasrid emirate of Granada, the last Muslim-ruled polity in Iberia, by the Crowns of Castile and Aragon in the Granada War (1482-1491), ending with the surrender of the city by Muhammad XII (Boabdil) on 2 January 1492 under Capitulations that guaranteed the Muslims' persons, property, law, and religious practice. Within a decade those guarantees were set aside: forced baptisms from 1499, the risings of 1499-1501, and the conversion orders of 1501-1502 ended the open practice of Islam in the kingdom of Granada and then in the Crown of Castile.
description:
By the later fifteenth century the Nasrid emirate of Granada was the last Muslim-ruled state in the Iberian peninsula, a tributary and frontier kingdom whose ruling house was divided by succession disputes between the emir Abu l-Hasan, his brother Muhammad al-Zaghal, and his son Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad (Muhammad XII, called Boabdil in Castilian). The war began in 1482, when a Castilian force took Alhama. Over the following decade the armies of Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile reduced the kingdom district by district, taking Loja, Velez-Malaga, Malaga, and Baza, while al-Zaghal surrendered Almeria and Guadix (1489). The narrative of the fall in al-Maqqari's Nafh al-tib, compiled from the accounts of Granadan historians, records most surrenders as capitulations, the inhabitants often withdrawing to the capital; Malaga (1487), taken after a long siege, ended in the captivity of its population. Muhammad XII, who had been captured by the Castilians in 1483 and released as their vassal, held the city of Granada. In 1491 the Castilians besieged it and built the camp-town of Santa Fe before its walls.

With provisions failing, the city negotiated terms. The narrative in al-Maqqari reports that the inhabitants consulted their ulama, who advised them to see to their own safety, and that the Capitulations were drawn up on the model of those of Guadix, with further articles; it gives them as sixty-seven, among them that the Muslims be secure in their persons, families, and property; that 'their laws should be preserved as they were before, and that no one should judge them except by those same laws'; that their mosques and religious endowments remain 'as they were in the times of Islam'; that no muezzin be interrupted and no Muslim molested in prayer, fasting, or other religious observance; that those wishing to cross to North Africa be carried in the king's ships; that Christians who had become Muslims not be compelled to return to their former faith; and that the Pope be asked to assent. The same account reports that the Granadan deputies sought a papal guarantee and a royal oath, and that it was said the envoys were bribed to have that clause omitted. The Castilian court chronicle printed under Hernando del Pulgar's name, in a closing section its 1780 editor judged not to be Pulgar's, summarizes the agreement as one under which 'todos quedasen en su ley y en sus faciendas' with 'otros muchos capítulos', describes the giving of hostages, and narrates that on 2 January 1492 Muhammad XII came out to Ferdinand by the river Genil and handed over the keys, after which the cross and the royal standard were raised on the Torre de Comares and the Te Deum was sung. Muhammad XII was assigned a lordship, at Andarax in the Alpujarras according to al-Maqqari's narrative, in the valley of Purchena according to the Castilian chronicle, and soon afterwards crossed to North Africa. The narrative reports that he settled in Fez and died there in 940 AH (1533-34 CE), and al-Maqqari adds in his own voice that he saw the palaces the exiled sultan had built there in imitation of those of Granada and, visiting Fez in 1037 AH, met his descendants living on the charity of the mosques.

The terms were not maintained. Under the first archbishop of Granada, Hernando de Talavera, conversion was pursued mainly by persuasion; the arrival of Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros, archbishop of Toledo, in 1499 brought mass baptisms. The first coercive measures were directed at the elches, converts from Christianity to Islam, and their descendants, whom churchmen claimed for Christianity; the narrative in al-Maqqari itself reports this justification, that 'their priests had written [books] on the conveniency of compelling such Christians as had become Moslems to embrace their former religion', while calling the measures a breach of the treaty, the Christians having begun 'to infringe one by one the settled stipulations'. It records that the people of the Albaicin rose and that the rising was then treated as grounds for requiring conversion on pain of death. Revolts followed in the Alpujarras and the western sierras (1499-1501), which the Castilian authorities treated as voiding the Capitulations. By 1501 the Muslims of the kingdom of Granada had been baptized or had emigrated, and a royal pragmatic of February 1502 required the remaining Muslims (Mudejars) of the Crown of Castile to accept baptism or leave; the baptized population and their descendants became known as Moriscos. Modern historians, among them L. P. Harvey and David Coleman, trace the decade from a negotiated settlement that recognized Muslim law and worship to compulsory Christianization, and Coleman studies how the conquerors' project of building a Christian Granada shaped religious reform in the city across the sixteenth century. The modern Egyptian historian Muhammad 'Abd Allah 'Inan treats the fall and the Morisco period together, in a volume titled The End of al-Andalus and the History of the Christianized Arabs. In Spanish historiography 1492 is the conventional end of the 'Reconquista'; Martín Ríos Saloma distinguishes the term's several senses, among them a period 'desde la batalla de Covadonga en 718 hasta la conquista de Granada en 1492' and a historiographical category, and argues that 'el mito de la Reconquista se reinventó en el siglo xix'. This entry uses the term only as a historiographical label. The surrender at Granada is also the setting of the Alhambra Decree of 31 March 1492, which ordered the expulsion of the Jews of Castile and Aragon.
editorial_notes: HOME TRADITION (ADR-0010): this entry is filed under islam because it chiefly concerns the fall of a Muslim polity (the Nasrid emirate) and its Muslim community; this is a storage convention, not a claim that the event belongs to one tradition. The Castilian and Christian side is sourced in its own voice (the court chronicle) and through historians of Christian Granada, and the Jewish dimension of the same year is reached through the expulsion-from-spain relation rather than duplicated here. VOICES: the narrative of the fall in al-Maqqari's Nafh al-tib is compiled from earlier Granadan accounts (al-Maqqari cites 'the historians of that city'); al-Maqqari (d. 1041/1632), born in Tlemcen and resident in Fez, adds first-person observations of his own (the Fez palaces 'which we ourselves saw', his visit to Fez in 1037 AH), and the entry attributes those to him and the rest to 'the narrative'. NEUTRALITY: the terms of the Capitulations are reported from the texts that record them and attributed; the charge that the Granadan envoys were bribed is reported as the narrative's own 'it was reported', not as fact; the breach is described both in the narrative's words and through the Castilian justification it itself records (the claim on the elches) and the Castilian position that the risings voided the agreement (neutrality #1, #2, #11). The devotional register of both primary texts (the narrative's divine chastisement and 'infidels'; the chronicle's Te Deum) is the texts' own and is not adopted. 'Reconquista' is named as a contested historiographical term, with Ríos Saloma's analysis attributed and no verdict given. DATES: see the date note for the chronicle's internal looseness on the handover and for Gayangos's conversions (3 January 1492; A.D. 1538 for 940 AH, where 1533-34 is correct). The article count (sixty-seven) is the narrative's; modern editions distinguish an earlier Castilian text of the Capitulations dated 25 November 1491 and a later confirmation, which this entry does not attempt to reconcile. CHRONICLE AUTHORSHIP: the 1780 editor notes at this point that 'En el MS. del Escorial faltan los dos capítulos siguientes; y á la verdad no parecen de Pulgar', citing Galíndez de Carvajal's statement that Pulgar 'solo escribió hasta el año noventa'; the passage is therefore cited as the printed court-chronicle continuation, not as Pulgar's own text. SOURCING (neutrality #8, #9): (a) modern academic historians, Harvey 1990 and 2005, Coleman 2003, Ríos Saloma 2011; (b) primary texts from both sides, al-Maqqari's narrative (Gayangos's English version, public domain) and the Castilian court chronicle (1780 printing, public domain); (c) a modern Muslim historian, Muhammad 'Abd Allah 'Inan (Mohammad Abdullah Enan). No encyclopedias or tertiary sources. CONFIDENCE: the two primary texts were read directly for the passages used (al-Maqqari vol. 2, Book VIII ch. 7, pp. 381-391; the chronicle's ch. CXXXIII, around pp. 374-375) and are rated high for those passages, the chronicle's rating applying to the printed continuation; the introduction of Ríos Saloma's book (pp. 30-32, open-access UNAM edition) was read directly and is rated high; the other monographs were verified to exist and be on-topic through publisher, library, and review records but not read line by line, and are rated medium. In Gayangos's translation (vol. 2, p. 381) the sentence on the negotiation before the city's capture names the inhabitants of 'Baza', but the passage sits in the account of the siege of Malaga and closes with 'The taking of Malaga'; this entry reads it as referring to Malaga and flags the slip.

relations.note: The surrender of Nasrid Granada ended the last Muslim-ruled polity of al-Andalus, the Muslim-ruled Iberia whose history began with the conquest of 711.
The conquest of 711 began Muslim rule in Iberia; the surrender of Granada in 1492 is conventionally treated as its end.
The forced baptisms that followed the breach of the Capitulations (Granada 1499-1501, Castile 1502) created the community of baptized former Muslims and their descendants known as Moriscos.
The Moriscos, whose community took shape in the conversions that followed the fall of Granada, were expelled from the Spanish kingdoms by the decrees of Philip III (1609-1614).
The Alhambra Decree ordering the expulsion of the Jews of Castile and Aragon was signed by Ferdinand and Isabella at Granada on 31 March 1492, less than three months after the surrender of the city.

The Capitulations of Granada provided for Muslims to keep their law and worship under Christian rule, a late instance of the negotiated arrangements for religious minorities that discussions of convivencia address; their breach after 1499 ended that arrangement in the kingdom.

sources.citation: Ríos Saloma, Martín F. La Reconquista: una construcción historiográfica (siglos XVI-XIX). Madrid: Marcial Pons Historia; México: Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Instituto de Investigaciones Históricas, 2011. 352 pp. ISBN 978-84-92820-47-4. Academic study of how the term and idea of the Reconquista were constructed in Spanish historiography; its introduction distinguishes five senses of the term, including a period 'desde la batalla de Covadonga en 718 hasta la conquista de Granada en 1492' and 'una categoría historiográfica', and argues that 'el mito de la Reconquista se reinventó en el siglo xix'. The introduction (pp. 30-32) was read directly in the open-access UNAM digital edition (2016).
